newsitem.title: USA: Kevorkian arrested, charged in Ionia, Mich., suicide.
newsitem.headline: Kevorkian arrested, charged in Ionia, Mich., suicide.

text.p: Dr. Jack Kevorkian's legal troubles mounted Thursday when police arrested him and drove him handcuffed to this west-central Michigan town to face new assisted suicide charges.

Kevorkian was charged in District Court with violating Michigan's unwritten common law against assisted suicide for his role in the Aug. 30 death of 54-year-old Loretta Peabody, an Ionia resident initially thought to have died from natural causes.
The assisted suicide activist also was charged with two counts of practicing medicine without a license and conspiracy to assist in a suicide.

Kevorkian's involvement in Peabody's death was not known until police confiscated a videotape in a September raid of a Bloomfield Township, Mich., hotel room where Kevorkian was meeting with another patient.
The charges follow the convening of a grand jury earlier this week by Ionia County prosecutor Raymond Voet.
On Monday, Kevorkian admitted at a news conference that he consulted with Peabody, whose death became the 45th he has acknowledged attending since 1990.
Kevorkian's lawyer, Geoffrey Fieger, played videotapes showing Peabody, who suffered from multiple sclerosis, saying she could not endure her suffering any longer and wanted to die.
"I've fought this as long as I can fight this," Peabody was heard saying. Her husband and daughter Monday asked that authorities leave the case alone.
On Thursday morning, Kevorkian was shopping in the Detroit suburb of Waterford Township, Mich., when he was arrested by plainclothes officers.

Salesman Jason Whitten at the National Pawn Brokers Outlet said Kevorkian was at the store looking at electronic keyboards shortly before he was arrested. Kevorkian, an avid organist, was a regular customer, Whitten said.
"I noticed that he was surrounded by some gentlemen (outside the store) who handcuffed him and escorted him into a van," Whitten said.
Fieger called the surprise arrest "despicable" and said it was an act of political grandstanding by Voet.
"We would have surrendered Dr. Kevorkian if (Voet) would have wanted to charge him."

The 68-year-old retired pathologist has been acquitted by Detroit-area juries three times on assisted suicide charges since May 1994, based on an an emotional defence that he wanted to relieve suffering, not cause death.

Kevorkian, handcuffed and draped in an orange prison jacket as he was brought into the courthouse on a rainy afternoon, was asked by reporters if he was afraid he would face more a conservative jury in Ionia, a town of about 6,000 residents 30 miles east of Grand Rapids.
"I'm afraid of these Nazi goons," he said.
Kevorkian was freed on his personal recognisance after Fieger demanded his release and threatened that he would go on a hunger strike if kept in custody.
If convicted on the felony assisted suicide charge, Kevorkian faces up to five years in prison.
Last week, outgoing Oakland County Prosecutor Richard Thompson took a final shot at bringing Kevorkian to justice, filing 19 new criminal charges against him for 10 deaths he has attended since June.
David Gorcyca, who was elected as Thompson's successor on Tuesday, has said he is not sure whether he will pursue the charges when he takes office in January.
